biliary-tract-cancers.core: Progressive obstructive jaundice or a suspicious gallbladder lesion warrants anatomic staging and assessment for complete surgical removal.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Cholangiocarcinoma: **PSC**, choledochal cysts, chronic biliary inflammation, Clonorchis/Opisthorchis infection
Gallbladder carcinoma: gallstones, chronic cholecystitis, gallbladder polyps, older age
Porcelain gallbladder: malignancy risk varies with calcification pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, weight loss; ↑direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase
Painless jaundice, dilated intrahepatic ducts, collapsed gallbladder → **hilar obstruction** (Klatskin tumor)
Gallbladder cancer often incidental after cholecystectomy; advanced disease causes RUQ pain or liver invasion
Fever, rigors, hypotension with obstruction → superimposed acute cholangitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Usually adenocarcinoma arising from chronically injured biliary epithelium
Infiltrative strictures obstruct bile flow; local vascular encasement may prevent resection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ RUQ ultrasound first → contrast CT/MRI + **MRCP** to map ducts, vessels, metastases
ERCP: brush cytology/biopsy and drainage; negative brushing does not exclude malignancy
CA 19-9 supportive only: elevated with benign obstruction, absent in some patients
Avoid transperitoneal biopsy of suspected transplant-eligible perihilar disease; tumor seeding may preclude transplant

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cholangitis → IV antibiotics + urgent biliary drainage; selective decompression for severe obstruction
Resectable disease → site-specific operation; consider adjuvant capecitabine
★ Advanced disease → gemcitabine/cisplatin + durvalumab or pembrolizumab; palliative stenting
Selected localized unresectable perihilar tumors → specialized neoadjuvant/transplant protocol

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent cholangitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis, hepatic failure
ERCP pancreatitis, stent occlusion; postoperative bile leak

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat liver fluke infection; avoid raw freshwater fish in endemic regions
PSC surveillance through hepatology; investigate new dominant/relevant strictures promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: episodic biliary pain, duct stone
IgG4 cholangitis: autoimmune pancreatitis, elevated IgG4
Pancreatic head cancer: pancreatic mass, double-duct dilation

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery (**adhesions**, leading cause), incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Complete → **obstipation**, no flatus; partial may still pass stool/diarrhea, not excluding obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels, no rectal gas; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain
★ Massive colonic distention + **coffee-bean (inverted-U) loop** on radiograph → sigmoid volvulus
Pregnancy: plain radiograph acceptable first (minimal fetal dose); MRI if unclear; do not delay

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs
Ileus: hypoactive/absent sounds, gas throughout bowel including rectum
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: dysmotility, dilated loops without transition point

table.title: Large-bowel branches
rows: Sigmoidoscopic detorsion, rectal tube → same-admission resection

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

table.title: Tumor distinctions
rows: Months of headache, deficits; necrotic, crosses corpus callosum
Woman; extra-axial, uniform enhancement, dural tail; parasagittal
Child; midline cerebellar mass; CSF drop metastases
CPA; insidious, high-frequency unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Child; ataxia, nystagmus, head tilt, cranial neuropathies

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

breast-cancer-screening.name: Breast cancer screening
breast-cancer-screening.scope: USPSTF screening mammography recommendations, age-based intervals, high-risk screening (BRCA, prior chest radiation, breast MRI), clinical breast exam, diagnostic evaluation of abnormal screening
breast-cancer-screening.core: USPSTF recommends biennial mammography from ages 40–74 for average-risk women; symptoms require diagnostic evaluation regardless of screening schedule.

rows.label: Who
items: Average risk includes family history or dense breasts without a defined high-risk syndrome
★ BRCA pathogenic variant, young chest irradiation or lifetime risk **≥20–25%** → high-risk pathway

rows.label: Start/stop
items: Age ≥75: insufficient USPSTF evidence; individualize by health, life expectancy and preference
High risk: annual MRI plus mammography, typically around age 30; specialist-tailored earlier MRI
BRCA1/2: **bilateral mastectomy + salpingo-oophorectomy** = greatest risk reduction; tamoxifen weaker

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Digital mammography/tomosynthesis; **MRI supplements**, not replaces, high-risk mammography
Clinical breast examination and breast self-examination do not substitute for imaging

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ BI-RADS 0 → **diagnostic views/targeted ultrasound**; 4–5 → core needle biopsy
BI-RADS 3 → short-interval imaging, usually 6 months; 1–2 → routine interval
Palpable concerning mass with negative imaging → tissue assessment for clinical–radiologic discordance

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Older teaching: 50; **2024 USPSTF starts at 40**; other societies accept annual
Dense breasts alone: insufficient USPSTF evidence for routine supplemental ultrasound/MRI
Harms: false positives, biopsy, overdiagnosis; concerning mass needs evaluation despite normal mammogram

burn-injuries.name: Burn injuries
burn-injuries.scope: Superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness burns, total body surface area (Rule of Nines), fluid resuscitation (Parkland), smoke inhalation and airway edema, carbon monoxide/cyanide toxicity
burn-injuries.core: Burn severity depends on depth, affected surface area, location, and inhalation injury; airway threats and hypovolemia take priority over wound care.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Flames/scalds, electricity, chemicals; closed-space fires increase toxic inhalation risk
Older adults, children, impaired mobility/sensation; inconsistent injury history raises abuse concern

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hoarseness, stridor, oropharyngeal edema, soot** → threatened airway; skin burns may appear minor
CO: headache, confusion, syncope despite normal pulse oximetry
Cyanide: enclosed-fire exposure with cardiovascular collapse and severe lactic acidosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Capillary leak → intravascular depletion and edema; swelling progresses after initial presentation
CO impairs oxygen transport; cyanide blocks mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TBSA excludes superficial burns**; adult Rule of Nines: head/each arm 9%, each leg 18%
Anterior/posterior trunk 18% each, perineum 1%; own palm including fingers ≈1%; children → Lund-Browder
★ Inhalation/toxin concern → **ABG with co-oximetry**, lactate; normal PaO2 does not exclude CO
Electrical burn → ECG, CK, urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis; small surface injury may hide deep damage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway threat → **intubate**; burn center: full-thickness, ≥10% partial, critical-site, inhalation/electrical/chemical
CO → 100% oxygen; severe neurologic/cardiac toxicity or pregnancy → consider hyperbaric oxygen; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin
Lactated Ringer, no early colloid: **Parkland = 4 mL × kg × %TBSA** over 24 hours
Half by 8 hours from injury, remainder over 16; ABA now starts adults at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA

rows.label: Complications
items: Shock, AKI, infection, contractures, compartment syndrome; overresuscitation worsens edema
Restrictive chest/limb eschar → escharotomy; true compartment syndrome → fasciotomy
Prognosis: **inhalation injury** often raises mortality more than moderate TBSA or comorbidities

rows.label: Prevention
items: Titrate fluids to urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults; formula only starting estimate
Small burn: cleaning, **bacitracin**, nonadherent dressing, tetanus, analgesia, no IV bolus; no routine systemic antibiotics
★ **Stop exposure, remove jewelry, cool water**, prevent hypothermia; no ice
Smoke/CO detectors, safe water temperature, fire escape plan; early rehabilitation and range of motion

rows.label: Mimics
items: SJS/TEN: medication exposure, mucosal erosions, widespread epidermal detachment
Cellulitis: spreading warmth/erythema without immediate thermal exposure

table.title: Depth
rows: Moist blisters, brisk blanching, very painful

burn-injuries.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ABA burn resuscitation guideline 2024](https://academic.oup.com/jbcr/article/45/3/565/7458089); classic Parkland contrasted with current initial estimate.

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease
chronic-kidney-disease.scope: CKD progression, anemia of CKD (erythropoietin deficiency), mineral and bone disorder, uremic complications, volume overload, indications for emergent dialysis (AEIOU), vascular access
chronic-kidney-disease.core: Persistent kidney injury or reduced filtration causes progressive cardiovascular, metabolic and uremic complications; dialysis follows clinical indications rather than creatinine alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease, obstruction, recurrent AKI, inherited cystic disease
NSAIDs, smoking and uncontrolled proteinuria accelerate progression

rows.label: Clues
items: Early disease often asymptomatic; advanced disease → fatigue, pruritus, anorexia, edema
Uremia: confusion, myoclonus, pericardial friction rub, nausea or bleeding despite normal platelet count
Labs: normocytic anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, ↑phosphate, low/normal calcium

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nephron loss → hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons, proteinuria and fibrosis
↓Erythropoietin → anemia; phosphate retention/↓calcitriol → ↓calcium absorption → four-gland secondary hyperparathyroidism
Renal bone disease: ↓calcitriol → **deficient osteoid mineralization**, atraumatic fracture; ↑PTH → subperiosteal resorption

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **eGFR <60** or kidney-damage markers for **≥3 months** establishes CKD
Urine albumin/creatinine ratio, urinalysis, creatinine trend; ultrasound for size/obstruction
Stage by GFR and albuminuria; small echogenic kidneys support chronicity but are not universal
Monitor CBC, ferritin/TSAT, K, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and PTH

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Albuminuric CKD → **ACE inhibitor/ARB**; monitor creatinine/K; never combine both
SGLT2 inhibitor for T2DM or qualifying albuminuric CKD/HF, generally starting eGFR ≥20
Overload → salt restriction, furosemide; high phosphate → phosphorus restriction, sevelamer; severe hyperparathyroidism → calcitriol
Iron repletion before ESA for selected persistent anemia; correct clinically significant metabolic acidosis
★ **Dialysis (AEIOU)**: refractory acidosis/hyperkalemia/overload (anuria: no diuretics), dialyzable toxins, uremic complications

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiovascular death, fractures, severe hyperkalemic arrhythmia, malnutrition
Dialysis access infection/thrombosis; rapid urea reduction → dialysis disequilibrium
Peritoneal dialysis + fever/abdominal pain → first **peritoneal fluid cell count, Gram stain, culture**

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Preserve arm veins; plan **AV fistula** before hemodialysis; temporary catheter for emergencies; early transplant referral
BP/glycemic control, avoid nephrotoxins, renal drug adjustment; hepatitis B vaccination before dialysis

rows.label: Mimics
items: AKI: acute creatinine change; may complicate established CKD
Prerenal azotemia: reversible perfusion deficit without persistent structural injury

chronic-venous-insufficiency.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
chronic-venous-insufficiency.scope: Varicose veins, stasis dermatitis, venous stasis ulcers, superficial thrombophlebitis, post-thrombotic syndrome
chronic-venous-insufficiency.core: Venous hypertension produces dependent edema, hemosiderin pigmentation, and shallow medial ankle ulcers that improve with elevation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior DVT, obesity, pregnancy, prolonged standing, older age, family history
Reduced calf-muscle pumping from immobility; previous leg trauma or venous surgery

rows.label: Clues
items: Aching/heaviness worsened by standing; varicosities, pitting swelling, preserved pedal pulses
Eczematous itching, lipodermatosclerosis, inverted champagne-bottle leg contour
★ **Irregular, exudative gaiter-region wound**; bilateral erythema without systemic illness favors stasis dermatitis
Superficial thrombophlebitis: focal erythema over a tender palpable venous cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Valve failure or outflow obstruction → reflux, capillary leakage, chronic inflammation
Post-thrombotic syndrome: residual obstruction and valvular injury following DVT

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous duplex ultrasound** evaluates reflux and obstruction; clinical examination often establishes diagnosis
★ **Ankle-brachial index before compression** when PAD suspected; <0.5 → avoid sustained compression
Nonhealing or atypical ulcer → biopsy for malignancy; sudden unilateral worsening → evaluate acute DVT
New superficial cord → assess clot length, proximity to deep junction, associated DVT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adequate arterial inflow → **compression bandaging/stockings + leg elevation**; walking activates calf pump
Ulcers: saline cleansing, moist absorbent dressings, debridement when needed
Stasis dermatitis: emollients + short-course topical steroid on intact skin; weeping → saline-soaked dressings, elevation
Symptomatic superficial reflux → endovenous ablation; moderate arterial disease → specialist-guided reduced compression
No antibiotics for colonization alone; cellulitis → systemic antibiotics; no routine diuretics without volume overload

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent ulceration, cellulitis, contact dermatitis; superficial clot can extend into deep veins
Chronic wounds rarely undergo squamous malignant transformation; new growth or bleeding warrants biopsy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight reduction, regular mobility, avoid prolonged dependent posture
Long-term compression after ulcer healing reduces recurrence; moisturize skin and treat venous reflux

rows.label: Mimics
items: Arterial ulcer: painful punched-out toes/lateral ankle, cool foot, weak pulses
Neuropathic ulcer: plantar pressure points, sensory loss, callus
Lymphedema: dorsal foot/toe swelling, later nonpitting thickened skin

table.title: Superficial thrombosis treatment
rows: Short distal segment, no high-risk features
≥5 cm long, >3 cm from deep junction

chronic-venous-insufficiency.evidence: Thrombosis checked 2026-10-30: [SVS/AVF/AVLS 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11523430/); wound care established teaching.

cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.name: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.scope: Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, esophageal varices, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma screening
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.core: Cirrhosis produces portal hypertension and synthetic failure; new ascites, bleeding, confusion or kidney injury signals decompensation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol, chronic HBV/HCV, metabolic steatotic liver disease; autoimmune/cholestatic disorders

rows.label: Clues
items: Splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, spider angiomas, jaundice, muscle wasting
Encephalopathy: **asterixis**; triggers GI bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives, hypokalemia, protein load
SBP may present only with subtle confusion or renal deterioration; fever/pain can be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fibrosis raises intrahepatic resistance; splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume
Portal collaterals bleed; impaired toxin clearance causes neuropsychiatric dysfunction
SBP: **intestinal bacterial translocation** into ascitic fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New/worsening or hospitalized ascites → **diagnostic paracentesis**; PMN **≥250/µL** → treat SBP
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension; send ascitic culture in bedside blood-culture bottles
HRS-AKI: exclude shock, nephrotoxins, obstruction and structural injury; assess volume response
MELD-Na/MELD 3.0 guides prognosis/transplant assessment
Encephalopathy clinical: **ammonia** not diagnostic; older exam questions may expect serum ammonia after normal head CT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Variceal bleed → resuscitate, **octreotide + ceftriaxone**, urgent endoscopic banding; refractory → TIPS
Ascites → sodium restriction, spironolactone ± furosemide; tense ascites → paracentesis, albumin if >5 L
★ SBP → **ceftriaxone**, albumin for high-risk renal/liver dysfunction; reassess response
Encephalopathy → lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day, rifaximin (add for recurrence); correct trigger; no sedatives
HRS → stop diuretics/nephrotoxins, **terlipressin + albumin** after volume assessment; monitor hypoxia; transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: HCC, recurrent infection, malnutrition, hepatopulmonary syndrome; TIPS can worsen encephalopathy
Avoid NSAIDs, sedatives and unnecessary fluid loading; INR alone poorly predicts procedural bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Ultrasound + AFP every 6 months** for HCC surveillance in eligible cirrhosis
Carvedilol for clinically significant portal hypertension when tolerated; banding if indicated and beta blocker unsuitable
After SBP → antibiotic prophylaxis; alcohol abstinence, hepatitis vaccines, adequate protein intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiac ascites: high SAAG with ascitic protein ≥2.5 g/dL
Malignant/TB ascites: usually low SAAG

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → **cricopharyngeal myotomy + diverticulectomy** or endoscopic septotomy; no dilation or blind NG tube

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**
Post-cholecystectomy jaundice + dilated ducts → retained stone/duct injury → **ERCP**; HIDA only for bile leak

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency
**Melena**, elevated BUN/creatinine ratio → upper source; bilious NG aspirate argues against upper bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit
Rectal bleeding mixed with stool, age ≥45 → colonoscopy; negative FOBT does not exclude neoplasia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Exsanguination or post-crystalloid shock → **RBCs** regardless of hemoglobin, not vasopressors; cardiac ischemia → higher threshold
Severe anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; uncontrolled varices → balloon tamponade as temporary bridge only
Failed endoscopy → IR/surgery; massive unlocalized lower bleeding → **total abdominal colectomy**, not segmental
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

table.title: Source-specific branches
rows: Postretching tear; Boerhaave instead: chest pain, crepitus
Liver trauma + jaundice; blood from ampulla

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder
Hysterectomy/pelvic surgery → ureteral ligation: flank pain, fever, unilateral hydroureteronephrosis; not pyelonephritis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention, perineal/scrotal hematoma or high-riding prostate → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Blunt flank trauma → **urinalysis**; stable, no hematuria → **no further testing** unless high-energy deceleration
Stable gross hematuria, or microscopic + hypotension → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images, not laparotomy
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; absent flow or high clinical suspicion → immediate exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

hemolytic-anemias.name: Hemolytic Anemias
hemolytic-anemias.scope: autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold agglutinins), hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, DAT/Coombs testing, peripheral smear, complications
hemolytic-anemias.core: Reticulocytosis, elevated LDH/indirect bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin suggest hemolysis; DAT and smear identify the mechanism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune disease, CLL, drugs → immune hemolysis; infections can trigger cold-antibody disease
Family history → inherited membrane/enzyme defect; oxidants, fava beans or infection trigger G6PD crises
Coombs-negative newborn jaundice after maternal oxidant drug → consider G6PD; X-linked, Mediterranean ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine; splenomegaly suggests chronic extravascular destruction
Severe intravascular lysis → hemoglobinuria, back pain, AKI; hemoglobin decline can outpace reticulocyte response
Spherocytes occur in hereditary and warm immune disease; morphology alone cannot distinguish them
Childhood gallstones + splenomegaly + family history → hereditary spherocytosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extravascular: splenic/hepatic macrophage clearance; intravascular: RBC destruction within circulation
Free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin; marrow compensates unless infection, deficiency or marrow failure limits production
Hereditary spherocytosis: ankyrin/spectrin cytoskeleton defect changes RBC shape → trapping in splenic red pulp

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin**, peripheral smear
★ **DAT/Coombs** detects immune coating; negative test redirects toward nonimmune causes
Hereditary spherocytosis → eosin-5-maleimide binding test; usually normocytic, normochromic; ↑MCHC supports
G6PD activity can be falsely normal during crisis/after transfusion → repeat after recovery
Schistocytes → evaluate microangiopathy/mechanical destruction urgently, including platelet count and renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe symptomatic anemia → **transfuse promptly** with blood-bank coordination; do not await perfect compatibility
Warm AIHA → glucocorticoids; refractory → rituximab or selected splenectomy
Cold disease → warmth, treat cause; rituximab-based treatment when symptomatic; steroids usually ineffective
G6PD → stop oxidant, treat trigger, supportive transfusion when severe
Hereditary spherocytosis → folate; selected severe disease → splenectomy after immunization

rows.label: Complications
items: Pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis; chronic immune disease increases thrombosis risk
Splenectomy → encapsulated infection and thrombosis; intravascular disease → renal injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ G6PD: avoid **dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, sulfonamides** and other oxidants
Before splenectomy: pneumococcal/meningococcal/Hib vaccines; infection education and selected antibiotic prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blood loss: reticulocytosis without hemolytic chemistry
Gilbert syndrome: isolated indirect bilirubin without anemia

table.title: Mechanism signatures
rows: Bite cells; Heinz bodies on supravital stain

hemolytic-anemias.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology teaching.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage (most common) or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids/vitamin A supplements

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late, compensatory; treat ICP, not BP
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema
IIH: **impaired CSF resorption** at arachnoid granulations; ventricles normal/small, no obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings → **LP**: normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction
Recent shunt revision + fever + neutrophilic CSF → **shunt infection**, not community meningitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway/intubation first**, head elevation, IV **hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis; PSC particularly associated with UC
Erythema nodosum: tender nonulcerating nodules; **pyoderma gangrenosum**: rapid painful violaceous ulcer, purulent base
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention, colon >6 cm → **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → CT/MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Partial SBO, suspected stricture → enterography; older exam questions may expect **water-soluble small-bowel follow-through**
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Moderate/severe flare without obstruction or abscess → **prednisone** induces remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression
UC with colorectal cancer → **total proctocolectomy**, not segmental colectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas (enterovaginal → vaginal flatus), strictures, obstruction in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Terminal ileal Crohn → B12 deficiency, **bile salt malabsorption** → steatorrhea
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

table.title: Distribution and outpatient treatment
rows: RLQ mass, cobblestones, perianal disease, granulomas
Bloody diarrhea, tenesmus; friability, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate (own case), reason, communicate**; decision-specific, fluctuating
Competence: legal; diagnosis, age, alcohol use, incarceration, disagreement alone ≠ incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, even if life-saving or pregnant; avoid coercion, abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient
Refusing one therapy (blood) ≠ refusing all; provide other indicated care, including surgery

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no surrogate/directive/verified refusal → implied consent to treat
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or changed risk → renewed consent; consent revocable anytime before procedure

table.title: Who decides
rows: Ask whom to involve; facilitate promptly; no override
Minor decides; no parental consent (state law varies)
Parents seek unproven remedy for child
Continue proven therapy; investigate remedy; CPS not first
Close; discuss after waking; no next-of-kin consent
Autonomy ≠ entitlement; physician refuses, explains, offers alternatives

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

knee-injuries.name: Knee injuries
knee-injuries.scope: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear, collateral ligaments, meniscal tears, knee dislocation, popliteal artery injury, Ottawa knee rules
knee-injuries.core: Knee trauma assessment starts with neurovascular safety and fracture risk, then uses mechanism, effusion timing, and targeted ligament or meniscal tests.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pivoting/cutting sports, contact trauma, dashboard impact, hyperextension
Older age, osteoporosis, and inability to bear weight increase fracture probability

rows.label: Clues
items: Immediate large effusion suggests hemarthrosis; delayed swelling and catching suggest meniscal injury
★ **Gross deformity or spontaneously reduced dislocation** → popliteal artery injury risk
Cool foot, weak pulses, paresthesia, escalating pain → vascular compromise or compartment syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament disruption → instability; displaced meniscal fragment → mechanical locking
Knee dislocation may stretch/tear popliteal artery despite restored alignment and initially palpable pulses

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Neurovascular examination before and after reduction**; ABI assesses arterial injury
★ ABI **<0.9, abnormal pulses, or pre-reduction deficit → CT angiography**; hard ischemic signs → vascular intervention
Normal ABI/pulses, no prior deficit → serial vascular checks, not immediate discharge
Ottawa: age ≥55, isolated patellar/fibular-head tenderness, flexion <90°, or inability four-step weight-bearing → radiographs
MRI for soft-tissue injury after fracture evaluation; locked knee → prompt orthopedic assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Dislocation → **urgent reduction before angiography**, immobilization, orthopedic/vascular consultation
Initial sprain → ice/compression, analgesia, protected weight bearing then early rehabilitation
Isolated collateral sprain → hinged brace + rehabilitation; many PCL injuries managed nonoperatively
ACL rupture with athletic demands/persistent instability or combined injury → reconstruction discussion
Displaced locked meniscal tear → arthroscopy; degenerative tears without locking usually exercise-based rehabilitation

rows.label: Complications
items: Missed arterial injury → limb loss; peroneal nerve injury → foot drop
Chronic instability, recurrent meniscal injury, posttraumatic osteoarthritis, stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Neuromuscular landing/pivot training, strength and balance rehabilitation before sport return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Patellar dislocation: lateral patellar displacement, often spontaneous reduction
Septic arthritis: atraumatic hot effusion, fever; urgent aspiration
Patellofemoral pain/instability: running, stairs, sitting → anterior pain; crepitus, genu valgum, lax patella; no effusion unless acute dislocation
Osgood-Schlatter: growth-spurt athlete, chronic tibial tubercle pain; traction apophysitis, tendon-insertion microfractures

table.title: Mechanism and examination
rows: Joint-line tenderness; McMurray: click on rotation/extension; Thessaly

knee-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic trauma and Ottawa knee principles.

mesenteric-ischemia.name: Mesenteric ischemia
mesenteric-ischemia.scope: Acute mesenteric ischemia, chronic mesenteric ischemia, ischemic colitis, CTA abdomen, colonoscopy
mesenteric-ischemia.core: Intestinal hypoperfusion causes severe abdominal pain; early examination and lactate may appear deceptively reassuring.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: AF, recent MI, valvular disease → embolism; diffuse atherosclerosis → arterial thrombosis
Shock, heart failure, vasopressors → nonocclusive ischemia; hypercoagulability → mesenteric venous thrombosis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain out of proportion** to abdominal examination; sudden onset especially with embolism
Nausea, diarrhea, later bloody stool; guarding/rebound suggests transmural infarction
Right-sided colonic disease or severe pain without bleeding → investigate proximal mesenteric occlusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen supply failure injures mucosa before serosa; bacterial translocation and necrosis follow
Collateral flow usually protects intestine until acute major occlusion or multivessel chronic disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CTA abdomen/pelvis with arterial and venous phases** immediately for suspected acute ischemia
Do not delay lifesaving contrast imaging solely because of renal dysfunction
CBC, metabolic panel, lactate/ABG; **rising lactate** → severe hypoperfusion; normal early value does not exclude disease
Avoid colonoscopy with peritonitis, perforation, or suspected gangrene; minimal insufflation when safe

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute mesenteric: NPO, **IV saline, piperacillin-tazobactam, unfractionated heparin**; urgent vascular/surgical consult
★ **Peritonitis or infarcted bowel → emergency laparotomy**, resect nonviable bowel and restore flow
Arterial occlusion without peritonitis → urgent endovascular/open revascularization based on anatomy and expertise
Nonocclusive disease → restore perfusion, reduce vasoconstrictors; selected catheter-directed papaverine
Isolated mesenteric venous thrombosis without infarction → anticoagulation

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, multiorgan failure, death
Short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection; reperfusion injury, recurrent thrombosis
Ischemic colitis can heal with segmental stricture

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Anticoagulate AF when eligible**; smoking cessation, statin, atherosclerotic risk reduction
Treat low-flow triggers promptly; thrombophilia evaluation for selected venous thrombosis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Infectious colitis: exposure/fever, stool pathogen identification
Pancreatitis: epigastric/back pain with lipase elevation
Perforated viscus: early rigid abdomen/free air; bowel obstruction: transition point on CT
Aortoenteric fistula: months-years after aortic graft, herald then massive upper GI bleed

table.title: Chronic disease versus colonic ischemia
rows: Postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss
Cramps then hematochezia; older, low-flow, post-AAA repair
Fluids, bowel rest; ceftriaxone/metronidazole if moderate/severe

mesenteric-ischemia.evidence: Colonic disease checked 2026-10-30: [ACG colon ischemia guideline](https://acgcdn.gi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/ACG-Colon-Ischemia-Guideline-Summary.pdf); acute mesenteric treatment: established emergency framework.

methemoglobinemia.name: Methemoglobinemia
methemoglobinemia.scope: Oxidizing agents (dapsone, benzocaine, nitrates), chocolate-brown blood, pulse oximetry saturation gap, PaO2 normal, methylene blue, vitamin C
methemoglobinemia.core: Cyanosis that barely improves with oxygen despite adequate dissolved arterial oxygen suggests dysfunctional hemoglobin rather than primary lung failure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Oxidants: **dapsone, benzocaine, nitrates/nitrites**; also prilocaine and some industrial chemicals
Infants exposed to nitrate-contaminated well water; congenital cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Chocolate-brown blood**, gray-blue skin, pulse oximeter trending toward ~85%
Headache, dizziness, tachycardia, dyspnea; severe exposure → confusion, seizures, arrhythmias, coma
Symptoms occur at lower levels with anemia or cardiopulmonary disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hemoglobin iron oxidized Fe2+ → Fe3+; oxidized sites cannot bind oxygen
Remaining functional sites bind oxygen more tightly → impaired tissue unloading

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Co-oximetry** directly measures methemoglobin fraction; obtain venous or arterial blood
Normal PaO2 with falsely reassuring calculated ABG saturation → saturation gap versus measured pulse oximetry
Routine blood gas oxygen saturation calculation cannot exclude dyshemoglobinemia
Check CBC, lactate, exposure history; assess G6PD status when feasible without delaying urgent management

rows.label: Tx
items: Stop exposure, give high-flow oxygen; mild asymptomatic cases → observation and serial levels
★ Symptomatic or MetHb ≥20–30% → **methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV**; lower threshold with limited reserve
★ **G6PD deficiency** → avoid methylene blue; ascorbic acid, specialist-guided exchange transfusion for severe disease
Methylene blue + serotonergic drugs → serotonin toxicity risk; seek toxicology advice
Refractory severe disease → exchange transfusion or hyperbaric oxygen; monitor for dapsone-associated rebound

rows.label: Complications
items: Tissue hypoxia, lactic acidosis, cardiovascular collapse, neurologic injury
Excess methylene blue can cause hemolysis and paradoxical worsening

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid recurrent oxidant exposure; document offending drug and counsel about OTC topical anesthetics
Safe infant water supply; medical alert identification for hereditary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Carbon monoxide: pulse oximetry often falsely normal; elevated carboxyhemoglobin
Sulfhemoglobinemia: sulfur exposure, persistent cyanosis, no response to methylene blue
Pulmonary hypoxemia: reduced PaO2 generally tracks impaired oxygenation

neck-trauma.name: Neck trauma
neck-trauma.scope: Penetrating neck trauma, zone I-III neck injuries, blunt vascular injury, hard vs soft signs of vascular injury
neck-trauma.core: Airway and hemorrhage take priority in neck injury; physiology and examination guide intervention more than the wound’s anatomic zone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Stab/gunshot wounds penetrating platysma; high-energy blunt trauma, hanging, cervical hyperextension
Cervical spine fractures, basilar skull fracture or neck seat-belt injury with concerning findings → vascular-injury risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hard signs**: pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, bruit/thrill, shock or focal neurologic deficit
Airway compromise: stridor, major air leak, rapidly increasing swelling; possible occult laryngotracheal injury
Soft signs: minor hemoptysis, dysphagia, nonexpanding hematoma, historical bleeding; stable findings still require evaluation
Delayed stroke, headache or partial Horner syndrome may follow blunt carotid dissection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Arterial laceration/intimal flap → hemorrhage, emboli, stroke; carotid → aphasia, contralateral weakness; vertebral → posterior signs
Aerodigestive disruption permits obstruction, contamination and mediastinal infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable penetrating injury with soft signs/concerning trajectory → **CT angiography** of neck
Suspected esophageal injury → contrast esophagram and/or endoscopy; negative CTA alone may miss small perforation
Suspected laryngotracheal injury → flexible laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy; assess cervical spine in blunt trauma
Blunt cerebrovascular screening → CTA according to injury pattern and neurologic findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/hard signs → **airway control and immediate operative exploration**, no imaging delay
Direct pressure for hemorrhage, blood-product resuscitation; avoid blind clamping/probing
Threatened distorted airway → expert intubation with surgical-airway backup; avoid repeated traumatic attempts
★ Stable blunt dissection → **antiplatelet or anticoagulation** when bleeding risk permits; vascular consultation
Esophageal perforation → NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent source control

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, airway loss, exsanguination; pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, mediastinitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Spinal motion restriction for suspected cervical injury; restraints and violence-risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Superficial wound: platysma intact; still examine surrounding structures
Isolated soft-tissue hematoma: no vascular/aerodigestive lesion after evaluation

table.title: Traditional zones
rows: Base of neck; subclavian artery; difficult thoracic-inlet exposure

nephrolithiasis.name: Nephrolithiasis
nephrolithiasis.scope: Renal colic, calcium oxalate, uric acid, struvite, cystine, drug-induced stones, noncontrast CT, medical expulsive therapy, surgical indications
nephrolithiasis.core: Sudden colicky flank pain radiating toward the groin with hematuria suggests a ureteral stone; infection plus obstruction is an emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low urine volume, high sodium intake, family history, obesity, gout
Hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, recurrent urinary infection; low citrate, genetic defects

rows.label: Clues
items: Restlessness, nausea/vomiting, CVA tenderness; hematuria may be absent
★ **Fever, pyuria, hypotension, AKI, anuria** → infected or function-threatening obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Urinary supersaturation → crystal formation; obstruction raises ureteral pressure and provokes spasm
Ileal resection/Crohn → fatty acids bind calcium → **colonic oxalate absorption** → calcium oxalate stones

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis + culture if infection suspected**, creatinine, pregnancy test when relevant
★ Nonpregnant adult → **low-dose noncontrast CT**; pregnancy/children → renal ultrasound first
KUB misses radiolucent uric acid stones; radiographic invisibility does not exclude ureteral obstruction
Analyze passed stone; recurrent/high-risk disease → serum evaluation and 24-hour urine

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ketorolac** for analgesia, ondansetron for nausea, normal hydration; avoid forced high-volume fluids during obstruction
Small uncomplicated stones, pain controlled, afebrile → discharge, oral fluids, analgesia; distal 5–10 mm → consider tamsulosin
★ Infection + obstruction → **urgent stent or nephrostomy + IV antibiotics**; delay definitive stone removal
Intervene for uncontrolled pain, persistent obstruction, renal deterioration, large stone, or failed passage
Ureteroscopy/shock-wave lithotripsy selected by stone; >2 cm/staghorn → percutaneous nephrolithotomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis/urosepsis, recurrent stones, renal loss
Procedures → bleeding, infection, ureteral injury; tamsulosin → orthostasis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Aim **urine volume ≥2–2.5 L/day**, normal dietary calcium, low sodium, moderate animal protein
Recurrent calcium stones/hypercalciuria → chlorthalidone; hypocitraturia → potassium citrate
Do not restrict dietary calcium routinely; calcium with meals reduces enteric oxalate absorption

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: older patient, hemodynamic instability, aortic dilation
Pyelonephritis: fever/constant pain; torsion/ectopic pregnancy: genital/pelvic findings

table.title: Stone clues and targeted prevention
rows: Indinavir CT-occult; atazanavir CT-visible; topiramate promotes alkaline urine

nephrolithiasis.evidence: Not checked online; established stone evaluation and prevention principles.

normal-pediatric-variants.name: Normal pediatric variants
normal-pediatric-variants.scope: Thymic sail sign on chest radiograph, physiologic genu varum and valgum, tibial torsion, infantile hemangioma
normal-pediatric-variants.core: Age-appropriate anatomy and growth can resemble disease; symmetry, normal function, and expected evolution support reassurance instead of unnecessary intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Normal skeletal alignment changes with development; familial rotational profiles are common
Infantile hemangiomas more frequent with prematurity, low birth weight and female sex

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Symmetric painless findings with normal growth/function** favor physiologic variation
Asymmetry, pain, progression, short stature or abnormal neurologic examination → pathologic evaluation
Hemangiomas appear in first weeks, proliferate rapidly during infancy, then gradually involute
Periocular, airway/beard-distribution, ulcerating or large segmental lesions are high-risk, not simple cosmetic variants

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Growth remodels lower-limb alignment/rotation; normal thymic tissue may silhouette against the lung
Hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor with proliferative and involution phases, distinct from vascular malformation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symmetric limb variant → **clinical examination**, growth review and rotational profile
Imaging for red flags, atypical age or suspected metabolic bone disease; not routine physiologic bowing
Typical hemangioma → clinical diagnosis; ≥5 cutaneous lesions → hepatic ultrasound
Large segmental facial/lumbosacral lesion → evaluate associated structural anomalies with specialist guidance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance and observation** for physiologic alignment, thymic appearance, toddler genital self-touching without abuse signs
Special shoes/braces do not correct internal tibial torsion; persistent severe functional deformity → orthopedics
★ High-risk hemangioma → **early referral, oral propranolol**; selected superficial lesions → topical timolol
Give propranolol with feeds, hold during poor intake/vomiting; monitor bradycardia and hypoglycemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary imaging, bracing or surgery; hemangioma → ulceration, amblyopia, airway obstruction or residual skin change
Multiple hepatic hemangiomas → high-output heart failure or consumptive hypothyroidism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blount disease: progressive asymmetric tibial bowing; rickets: widened wrists, abnormal mineralization
Mediastinal mass: mass effect/distortion rather than soft thymic contour

normal-pediatric-variants.evidence: Hemangioma guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2019 guideline](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/143/1/e20183475/37268/Clinical-Practice-Guideline-for-the-Management-of); skeletal variants: established teaching.

table.title: Expected developmental patterns
rows: Varum to toddler; valgum peaks age 3–4
Yellow papules on erythematous base; trunk, well neonate
Resolves in days; reassure, no cultures
Bilateral nocturnal calf pain; normal exam, massage relieves
Blue hands, feet, perioral; pink mucosa, normal SpO2
Benign, first 24–48 hours; warmer if cold

nutritional-deficiencies.name: Nutritional deficiencies
nutritional-deficiencies.scope: Vegan diet nutrient risks, tea-and-toast diet, vitamin and mineral supplementation, clinical manifestations
nutritional-deficiencies.core: Restricted intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements produce characteristic mucocutaneous, neurologic, hematologic, and skeletal findings; identify the missing nutrient and its cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupplemented vegan diet: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc risks
Tea-and-toast diet, alcohol misuse, food insecurity, restrictive eating, institutionalization
Bariatric surgery, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bowel disease → specific or fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor wound healing, bruising, oral changes, neuropathy, bone pain; mixed deficiencies commonly coexist
★ **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia** in malnutrition → thiamine deficiency; complete triad often absent
Night blindness → vitamin A; bleeding with prolonged PT → vitamin K
Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia → niacin; periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, dysgeusia → zinc (TPN, penicillamine)

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient cofactors impair energy metabolism, collagen formation, hematopoiesis, or mineralization
Low intake differs from malabsorption: replacement route and lasting supplementation must match the mechanism
Vitamin D deficiency → ↓calcium absorption → **secondary hyperparathyroidism**: normal calcium at bone's expense

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diet and supplement history**, weight trend, oral/skin/neurologic examination; assess GI disease
CBC/ferritin, B12 ± methylmalonic acid, 25-OH vitamin D chosen by findings; avoid indiscriminate panels
Albumin is altered by inflammation/fluid status; not a stand-alone nutrition diagnostic test
Severely undernourished → baseline phosphate, Mg, K before nutritional rehabilitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke syndrome → **parenteral thiamine promptly**; do not await laboratory confirmation
B12 deficiency with neurologic signs/malabsorption → parenteral replacement; folate only after B12 assessment
Vitamin D/calcium for deficient intake or osteomalacia; iron replacement with evaluation for blood loss
Vitamin C for scurvy; oral balanced nutrition plus cause-directed supplementation and dietitian support
★ Severe malnutrition → **slow refeeding + thiamine**, close phosphate/K/Mg monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible B12 neurologic injury, fractures, anemia, infection susceptibility
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, respiratory failure; excess vitamin A → hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vegans → **reliable B12 supplementation**; fortified foods, calcium/vitamin D and iodine adequacy
Diversified diet, food access support, lifelong bariatric follow-up; avoid megadose supplementation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Scurvy versus vasculitis: perifollicular hemorrhage/corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, restricted produce intake
Hypothyroidism: fatigue and macrocytosis with elevated TSH

nutritional-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established nutritional deficiency and refeeding principles.

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.scope: Clinical diagnosis (Heberden/Bouchard nodes, activity-related pain), radiographic findings, nonpharmacologic therapy, oral and topical NSAIDs, injections
osteoarthritis.core: Activity-related joint pain with brief morning stiffness, crepitus and bony enlargement suggests degenerative joint disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, **obesity** (strongest modifiable), prior trauma, malalignment, repetitive occupational loading
Family history, particularly hand disease; obesity affects both mechanical and metabolic risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning stiffness generally **<30 minutes**; pain improves with rest early in disease
Knees, hips, first carpometacarpal, DIP and PIP commonly involved; MCP usually spared
Heberden nodes: DIP; Bouchard nodes: PIP; reduced motion and varus/valgus deformity
Hip disease: groin pain with restricted internal rotation; referred pain can localize to knee

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Articular cartilage loss, subchondral remodeling and osteophytes; low-grade synovial inflammation
Joint pain arises from innervated surrounding structures rather than aneural cartilage itself

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; imaging unnecessary for straightforward mild disease
Weight-bearing radiographs if uncertain, severe or worsening: asymmetric joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts
★ Hot acutely swollen joint → **arthrocentesis**; not an OA flare; mild cool effusion → x-ray, simple analgesic
OA fluid noninflammatory: usually WBC <2000/µL; inflammatory markers generally normal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **exercise, strengthening, weight loss**; cane contralateral to painful hip/knee
★ Knee/hand pain → **topical diclofenac**; oral NSAID if insufficient and renal/GI/CV risks acceptable
Acetaminophen if unable to use NSAIDs (older exam questions may expect it first); duloxetine for persistent pain
Intra-articular glucocorticoid for short-term relief; avoid routine opioids and hyaluronic acid injections
Severe pain/function loss despite conservative treatment → **joint replacement**

rows.label: Complications
items: Functional limitation, falls, reduced activity and secondary deconditioning
NSAIDs → GI bleeding, AKI, fluid retention; arthroplasty → infection or VTE

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Weight loss** best prevents knee OA, beyond exercise alone; conditioning, injury prevention; no complete joint rest

rows.label: Mimics
items: Rheumatoid arthritis: prolonged stiffness, boggy symmetric MCP/wrist synovitis, marginal erosions, DIP spared
CPPD: acute inflammatory flares, chondrocalcinosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe painful passive motion, positive synovial culture
Trochanteric bursitis: lateral hip pain over greater trochanter, not groin pain

osteoarthritis.evidence: Not checked online; established ACR/Arthritis Foundation principles.

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.scope: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma, CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, peritoneal carcinomatosis, germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors, surgical staging and cytoreduction, platinum-based chemotherapy
ovarian-cancer.core: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic symptoms, or an adnexal mass—especially after menopause—requires evaluation for an often late-presenting malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, nulliparity, BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome; family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Endometriosis associated with clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes; pregnancy and combined contraceptives reduce epithelial risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Older patient + ascites, large/fixed pelvic mass, weight loss, pleural effusion, obstruction → **epithelial** carcinoma
Young patient with rapidly enlarging mass → germ cell tumor; estrogen/androgen effects → stromal tumor
Postmenopausal bleeding with adnexal mass → consider estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor and endometrial disease
★ **Palpable ovary after menopause** → abnormal (ovaries atrophy); pelvic ultrasound

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Many high-grade serous tumors arise in distal fallopian tube epithelium
Transcoelomic seeding produces peritoneal/omental disease; hormone secretion depends on tumor lineage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** first; solid components, papillary projections, vascularity, ascites increase suspicion
★ **CA-125** supports risk assessment/monitoring, not diagnosis or average-risk screening
Young/complex mass → β-hCG, AFP, LDH; suspected stromal tumor → inhibin/sex hormones
Suspected malignancy → CT abdomen/pelvis/chest and gynecologic oncology; definitive histology and staging usually surgical
Isolated resectable mass → avoid aspiration; advanced disease → biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Epithelial carcinoma → **surgical staging/cytoreduction + carboplatin/paclitaxel** according to stage
Poor upfront surgical candidate → tissue confirmation, neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy, interval cytoreduction
Germ cell malignancy → fertility-sparing surgery when feasible; stage IA dysgerminoma may avoid chemotherapy
Higher-risk germ cell tumors → bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin
Selected BRCA/HRD-associated disease → PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum response

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, malignant obstruction, VTE; chemotherapy neuropathy/myelosuppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No routine CA-125/ultrasound screening** in asymptomatic average-risk patients
Genetic counseling/testing; hereditary high-risk patients → discuss risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endometrioma: cyclic pain, ground-glass ultrasound; CA-125 can rise
Meigs syndrome: benign ovarian fibroma plus ascites/pleural effusion; no peritoneal implants

table.title: Tumor markers
rows: Often bilateral; psammoma bodies; WT1+, p53 abnormal

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may show **double-duct** (bile + pancreatic) dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen
Massive watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, flushing

pancreatic-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established pancreatic oncology teaching.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
